prompt:
Patient is an 81-year-old woman, a retired school librarian who lives alone with her cat, with CAD (s/p CABG), paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (s/p ablation), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, osteoarthritis (knee replacements), and a history of alcohol use. Three weeks ago, the patient developed intense, bilateral, burning foot pain that occurs only at night. It is not exercise-induced. Exam reveals normal pedal pulses and decreased sensation to vibration at the great toes, light touch is intact. A CBC with differential, basic metabolic panel and B12 are normal. I suspected neuropathy but a trial of pregabalin 75 mg nightly has provided no relief. What are the next steps for work-up and symptomatic relief?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Order fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c to evaluate for diabetes or prediabetes.
Order a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test if initial glycemic testing is nondiagnostic.
Order TSH, with reflex free T4 if TSH is abnormal or central thyroid disease is suspected.
Order serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation; add serum free light chains when monoclonal gammopathy or amyloidosis is a particular concern.
Order serum methylmalonic acid despite the normal serum B12 level.
Order thiamine, vitamin B6, and folate levels given the alcohol history and neuropathic symptoms.
Order liver function tests before selecting potentially hepatotoxic neuropathic pain therapy.
Review the medication and supplement list for neurotoxic agents or excessive pyridoxine exposure.
Obtain a detailed alcohol history, including current intake, duration and pattern of use, and associated nutritional risk; a validated screen such as AUDIT-C may be used.
Perform a focused neurologic and foot examination including strength, reflexes, gait, and monofilament testing.
Order nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterize the neuropathy.
Perform skin punch biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density if small-fiber neuropathy remains suspected despite nondiagnostic electrodiagnostic testing.
Refer to neurology if symptoms persist, progress, or the initial evaluation is unrevealing.
Measure an ankle-brachial index if vascular disease remains a clinical concern.
Gradually titrate pregabalin to 75 mg twice daily or an equivalent renal-adjusted dose while monitoring sedation, dizziness, and edema.
Switch to duloxetine 30 mg daily with titration to 60 mg daily if pregabalin remains ineffective or poorly tolerated.
Use low-dose gabapentin with gradual titration as an alternative to pregabalin rather than as concurrent therapy.
Apply topical lidocaine 5% to the painful areas for up to 12 hours daily.
Apply low-concentration topical capsaicin to the painful areas three to four times daily.
Counsel on daily foot inspection, skin protection, and properly fitting footwear.
Provide fall-prevention counseling because neuropathy and sedating medications increase fall risk.
Refer to physical therapy for gait and balance training if instability is present.
Refer to podiatry if pressure lesions, skin or nail problems, deformity, or inability to perform safe foot care is identified.
Schedule follow-up within 2 to 6 weeks to review test results, pain response, and medication adverse effects.
Provide urgent return precautions for new weakness, rapidly ascending sensory loss, bowel or bladder dysfunction, foot ulceration, or falls.
Prescribe an opioid, including tramadol, for routine treatment of the neuropathic foot pain.
Initiate amitriptyline at 50 mg nightly or higher in this 81-year-old.
Start gabapentin at 900 mg three times daily without gradual titration.
Add gabapentin concurrently to ongoing pregabalin therapy.
Abruptly escalate pregabalin to at least 300 mg daily without titration or reassessment.
Recommend nightly alcohol use for analgesia or sleep.
Prescribe NSAIDs as treatment for the neuropathic pain.
Initiate systemic corticosteroids for presumed neuropathy without evidence of an inflammatory cause.
Discontinue indicated anticoagulation solely because neuropathy treatment is being considered.
Order CT angiography or invasive lower-extremity arteriography as an initial test without objective evidence of limb ischemia or a vascular intervention-planning indication.
Perform a sural or other peripheral nerve biopsy during the initial evaluation.
Arrange lumbar puncture during the initial evaluation without clinical or electrodiagnostic evidence suggesting an inflammatory, demyelinating, or infectious neuropathy.
Order lumbar spine MRI in the absence of back pain, radicular findings, weakness, or bowel or bladder symptoms.
Order a broad autoimmune serology panel without systemic features suggesting autoimmune disease.
Prescribe ongoing empirical pyridoxine supplementation at 100 mg/day or more for neuropathy without a specific indication.
